Why do sit-coms have laugh tracks?

So that you, the viewer, know it was funny and you should laugh. Makes it easier to mindlessly watch them. Sitcoms aren't meant to be heavy, resource intensive shows for you. They're for that brain dead time.
What's especially telling is watching commercials with the sound turned all the way down. The fake enthusiasm for the product is mind-boggling.

It's actually a little more complicated than "so you know it's funny, stupid".

Sitcoms originated in theater where you have people around you laughing. In principle, one function of the laugh track is to emulate that atmosphere. It seems to be the case that laughing together with other people actually makes comedy more enjoyable (humans are social animals after all).

Also, many, if not most sitcoms are actually filmed in front of audiences so they do have real laughter.

But of course there are those examples of shows that either think you're stupid or don't think their own jokes are funny and rely on group pressure to make you think it's funny. Just saying that this is not the original intent.

Not only do they have live audiences, they often also mix in professional laughers

http://www.wired.com/2012/01/humor-code-professional-laughers/
One reason they use laughter instead of random sounds is because laughter is contagious. Which you probably already knew, but, just thought I'd remind you.

Many years ago, people used to go to plays. Actors were used to working on a stage with an audience, and audiences got used to experiencing things as a group.

In the early days of radio, many shows were stage plays broadcasted live - that included the sounds of the audience, to replicate the experience of theater entertainment, even though you were at home.

Producers eventually figured out that real people can't always be counted on to laugh at exactly the right time, volume, and duration, though, and started tweaking the recordings of audience reactions, and sometimes even adding them where there were none.

Recorded audience reactions crossed the gulf into television, and the popularity there has waxed and waned since. It's not always canned - many sitcoms in the 90's, for instance, were actually filmed in front of a live audience, and so what you're hearing is somewhat genuine reactions (although usually coached, coaxed, coerced, and then later edited). Many times it's stock audio added in post-production, however.

As to why we're still doing it, at this point, it's mostly a stylistic decision. Some producers and directors like the classic, wholesome tone a laugh track adds.
